en.title: Streets and directions
en.summary: Asking the way and understanding the answer, with commands, prepositions and polite questions.

sections.title: About this lesson
paragraphs: Almost every visitor to a town has to ask the way. A good answer is made of short commands and small words that describe a route. In this lesson you will read one such conversation and look at three points of grammar: commands, prepositions and a polite way to ask.

sections.title: In context
paragraphs: A tourist stops a woman in the street in Edinburgh.

- **Tourist:** Excuse me, could you tell me where the station is?
- **Woman:** Of course. Go straight on along this road. Take the second turning on the left, and walk past the bank.
- **Tourist:** Is it far?
- **Woman:** No, it's about ten minutes on foot. Don't cross the bridge. At the traffic lights, turn right. The station is on your left, opposite the park.
- **Tourist:** Thank you very much.
- **Woman:** You're welcome.

sections.title: Grammar notes
paragraphs: **1. Commands use the base form of the verb.** There is no subject: **Go**, **Take**, **Turn**. For a negative command put Don't before the verb. Add please, or begin with Could you, to sound polite. See Introduction to Grammar: Moods.

| Kind | Example |
| --- | --- |
| positive command | **Go straight on.** |
| negative command | **Don't cross the bridge.** |
| polite request | **Could you tell me the way, please?** |
**2. Prepositions describe the route.** Each one shows a relation between the walker and a place. See Introduction to Grammar: Prepositions and cases.

| Preposition | Meaning | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| along | following the line of | **along this road** |
| past | going by, without stopping | **past the bank** |
| across | from one side to the other | **across the street** |
| opposite | facing | **opposite the park** |
| on the left, on the right | the side of you | **on your left** |

**3. A polite question keeps statement order.** After Could you tell me, the question word is followed by the subject and then the verb, as in a statement. We say **Could you tell me where the station is?** and not Could you tell me where is the station? See Introduction to Grammar: Conjunctions and linking clauses.

sections.title: Notice
paragraphs:
- Say **Excuse me** to get a stranger's attention, and **Sorry** if you bump into someone.
- A turning is a road that leaves the one you are on. British speakers say the second turning on the left, and Americans often say the second street on the left.
- The pavement is the path beside a road in British English. Americans call it the sidewalk.

sections.title: Culture note
paragraphs: In the United Kingdom people drive on the left, so when you cross a road you must look right first. In the United States people drive on the right.
